## Abstract

Syncope is a common complaint among Emergency Department patients. There are innumerable causes for syncope, and it poses a diagnostic challenge for Emergency Medicine (EM) physicians. Currently, several clinical decision rules (CDRs) for risk stratification of patients presenting with syncope depend on the circumstances surrounding the syncopal event, past medical history, vital signs, and results of basic diagnostic studies. However, the basis of these clinical decision tools is unreliable, such as the past medical history or nonspecific findings for various disease processes that can cause syncope. Given risk factors from unreliable sources, this raises the question: are we misclassifying our syncope patients? We posit in this narrative review that there is a role for a bedside diagnostic test, performed by the Emergency Medicine clinician, to assist with accurate risk stratification of syncope-causing pathologies: point-of-care cardiac ultrasound (POCCUS).

Keywords:

[syncope](/search?q=syncope); [point-of-care ultrasound](/search?q=point-of-care+ultrasound); [cardiac ultrasound](/search?q=cardiac+ultrasound); [pulmonary embolism](/search?q=pulmonary+embolism)

## 1. Background

Approximately 1–3% of all Emergency Department visits are for syncope or near-syncope [[1](#B1-jcm-15-03780)]. Syncope is defined as a transient loss of consciousness caused by cerebral hypoperfusion. The differential diagnosis for syncope is vast, from benign to life-threatening causes, and this poses a dilemma for EM clinicians. Because of this, syncope patients can undergo extensive evaluations, including inpatient stays. The cost of caring for syncope patients is high and growing, resulting in more than $2.4 billion in hospital costs per year [[2](#B2-jcm-15-03780)].

The current risk stratification tools factor in prodrome, age, electrocardiogram (EKG) findings, past medical history, laboratory studies, and vital signs. The Canadian Cardiovascular Society Position Statement in 2020 stated that syncope decision rules are not widely adopted because of important methodological limitations [[3](#B3-jcm-15-03780)], and these decision rules did not show better diagnostic or prognostic yield in outcome prediction when compared to clinician’s medical decision making alone [[4](#B4-jcm-15-03780)]. None of these clinical decision rules (CDRs) utilize imaging studies, and the imaging modality most well-suited for evaluating the cardiac status of syncope patients in the Emergency Department is the point-of-care cardiac ultrasound (POCCUS). There is currently a paucity of research in this area, and no established protocols to integrate POCCUS into evaluating patients with syncope to rule-in or rule-out a cardiac cause (arrhythmic, structural, cardiopulmonary).

POCCUS is one of the most commonly performed point-of-care ultrasound applications, used to evaluate chest pain, sepsis, hypotension, etc. [[5](#B5-jcm-15-03780)]. The assessment for hypotension, which includes inferior vena cava (IVC), gross left ventricular (LV) function, and pericardium, takes an average of 6 min to perform [[6](#B6-jcm-15-03780)]. Kapoor 1983 et al. showed that the 12-month mortality rate in syncope patients is 14%, with the highest percentage (30%) in patients with a cardiovascular cause [[7](#B7-jcm-15-03780)]. The European Society of Cardiology 2018 Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope recommends an echocardiogram for previous known heart disease or data suggestive of structural heart disease or syncope secondary to cardiovascular cause, which is done by a dedicated echocardiographer [[8](#B8-jcm-15-03780)], but there was no mention of cardiac ultrasounds performed by physicians at the bedside. Using point-of-care ultrasound at the bedside gives physicians the opportunity to improve and expedite the risk stratification of syncope patients who present with limited to no known medical history.

POCCUS is not currently incorporated into syncope evaluation frameworks due to: (1) the wide range prevalence (6–30%) of structural causes detectable by ultrasound [[9](#B9-jcm-15-03780)]; (2) the absence of standardized protocols and high-quality outcome data; and (3) variability in availability and operator dependence [[10](#B10-jcm-15-03780)]. However, increasing accessibility and expanding evidence in emergency settings suggest a potential evolving role as a targeted adjunct to current risk stratification tools to improve early identification of high-risk structural causes of syncope. Our narrative review will provide an overview of the current CDRs for syncope evaluation and recommend the integration of POCCUS into risk stratification tools.

## 2. Literature Review Approach

This narrative review was conducted using searches of PubMed for articles related to syncope, clinical decision rules, point-of-care ultrasound, and Emergency Department evaluation. Relevant studies were identified using combinations of keywords including “clinical decision rules,” “syncope,” “point-of-care ultrasound,” “cardiac ultrasound,” and “risk stratification.” Articles were selected based on relevance to the topic, with an emphasis on studies published in the last 20–25 years, as well as key guideline documents.

## 3. Current Risk Stratification Tools

Current risk stratification rules have significant limitations despite their widespread use in syncope risk stratification. Multiple CDRs rely heavily on patient-provided history and past medical history, as evidenced by [Table 1](#table_body_display_jcm-15-03780-t001). This approach is inherently flawed because patients cannot or do not provide accurate information surrounding the syncopal event. According to the 2018 census, approximately 27.5 million people lacked health insurance, increasing the risk of undiagnosed conditions due to limited access to care [[11](#B11-jcm-15-03780)]. Therefore, patients may be presenting to the ED with undiagnosed cardiac conditions that would not be detected from CDRs alone.

Moreover, all the CDRs include history of heart disease or heart failure as risk factors, and inclusion of these risk factors are dichotomous. However, this does not factor in progression or worsening or improvement of chronic conditions. Each of the CDRs also include abnormal EKGs or EKG changes as a risk factor for high-risk syncope, but the criteria are not consistent in the definition of “concerning” EKG changes. Additionally, changes in EKG can be unclear in their chronicity and may not contribute to the patient’s presenting symptoms, making EKG changes nonspecific. In Albassam et al.’s Rational Clinical Examination Systematic Review, of the 4317 patients included in their analysis, the finding of atrial fibrillation or flutter had a sensitivity of 0.13 (0.06–0.20) and a specificity of 0.98 (0.96–1.0) in detecting cardiac syncope [[12](#B12-jcm-15-03780)], which showed no single clinical or EKG finding can diagnose a cause for syncope. Risk stratification relies on the integration of multiple factors.

The San Francisco Syncope Rule is a widely cited tool to predict mortality in patients who present to the ED with syncope. Quinn et al. prospectively validated the San Francisco Syncope Rule (SFSR), and in their study of 791 consecutive syncope ED visits, the clinical decision rule was 98% sensitive and 56% specific for predicting adverse events [[13](#B13-jcm-15-03780)]. Their results showed 6.8% had a serious outcome after the ED visit, with arrhythmia and myocardial infarction at the top of the list. Cardiogenic syncope increases the risk of death by two-fold and also increases the risk of cardiovascular events [[14](#B14-jcm-15-03780)]. However, when the SFSR was applied to the elderly population of the ED (> age 65), the sensitivity decreased to 76.5%, and specificity also dropped to 36.8% [[15](#B15-jcm-15-03780)]. The elderly population is one of the most vulnerable populations we care for in the ED, and the ability to risk stratify this group of patients is critical, especially since other scores, such as the OESIL risk score, show that advanced age (>65 years) is one of the most predictive factors for death during the follow-up period [[16](#B16-jcm-15-03780)].

The OESIL (Osservatorio Epidemiologico sulla Sincope nel Lazio) risk score was prospectively validated by Colivicchi et al. with the primary endpoint as death from any cause within 12 months of study participation [[16](#B16-jcm-15-03780)]. Univariate predictors of death were age >65, syncope without prodromes, cardiovascular disease in clinical history, and abnormal EKG, sharing similar limitations of additional syncope rules. Syncope without prodrome has been considered as cardiac syncope, which yields a negative prognosis [[16](#B16-jcm-15-03780)].

The EGSYS (Evaluation Guidelines in Syncope Study) Score created by Brignole et al. 2006 based on the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) syncope management guidelines in 2006 utilized an interactive online decision-making system to assist physicians with the management of a patient who presents with syncope [[17](#B17-jcm-15-03780)]. Based on this, Del Rosso et al. prospectively validated the study in a multicenter study with 516 patients by determining the probability of cardiac syncope and mortality [[18](#B18-jcm-15-03780)]. Out of the 516 patients, the majority (67%) had a neurally mediated cause for syncope, and 79 (15%) patients had cardiac syncope, with 29% of those patients having a mechanical cause: acute coronary syndrome, aortic stenosis, pulmonary embolism, pericardial tamponade, and Eisenmenger syndrome. Several life-threatening structural causes of syncope—including tamponade, severe ventricular dysfunction, and right ventricular strain—are detectable using POCCUS, suggesting that integration of this modality may facilitate earlier bedside recognition [[19](#B19-jcm-15-03780)].

The Canadian Syncope Risk Score was more recently validated in a prospective, multicenter Emergency Department study by Thiruganasambandamoorthy et al. to guide management of syncope patients whose serious causes were not identified during their initial ED visit [[20](#B20-jcm-15-03780)]. In this study, 160 (4%) patients out of 3979 patients were found to have serious cardiac outcomes (arrhythmias, cardiac and non-cardiac serious outcomes, such as ACS, PE, etc.) identified during their initial ED evaluation. After their initial ED evaluation and disposition, 139 patients (3.6%) had serious outcomes.

Elderly patients who present with syncope have an increased risk of serious outcomes, and the FAINT Score was created to evaluate older adults who present with syncope to the Emergency Department [[21](#B21-jcm-15-03780)]. In this prospective observational study of 3177 older patients (60 or older), the FAINT Score had a sensitivity of 96.7% and specificity of 22.2% for predicting all-cause mortality or serious cardiac outcome (significant cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, new diagnosis of structural disease, or cardiac intervention) at 30 days. Interestingly, the FAINT score study did not include patients with pulmonary embolism, focusing only on cardiac outcomes. However, pulmonary embolism deserves to be discussed specifically, since syncope is the presenting symptom in up to 20% of patients with pulmonary embolism (PE) [[22](#B22-jcm-15-03780)].

Life-threatening causes of syncope are usually of cardiac origin, which includes acute PE [[23](#B23-jcm-15-03780)], and PE has been identified in 2.2–35% of syncope patients [[24](#B24-jcm-15-03780)]. The proposed mechanism for syncope secondary to PE is unclear, but the primary theory is that a large clot burden causes right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, leading to decreased cardiac output, hypotension, and decreased cerebral blood flow [[25](#B25-jcm-15-03780)]. In patients with acute PE and syncope, there is a strong association between syncope and cardiogenic shock and low systolic blood pressure (<90 mmHg) [[24](#B24-jcm-15-03780)]. Because pulmonary embolism is a common disease, seen in 1 in 1000 patients [[26](#B26-jcm-15-03780)], and 1 in 6 patients with PE present with syncope, it is important to identify this patient subset [[27](#B27-jcm-15-03780)]. In a recent meta-analysis, de Winter et al. concluded that there is an association between short-term mortality and syncope in patients with PE [[22](#B22-jcm-15-03780)]. There is a 4% increase in short-term mortality when patients present with syncope in the setting of PE.

The current clinical decision rules demonstrate several shortcomings. They are limited in evaluation of mechanical causes of syncope, do not factor in explicit risks or findings for pulmonary embolism, utilize historical features that have questionable accuracy, dependent on patient-provided information, and do not account for progression of underlying diseases and exacerbations. This is an area where bedside cardiac ultrasound can provide both sensitive and specific information to direct management and augment current CDRs.

## 4. Point-of-Care Cardiac Ultrasound

The prognosis of syncope is largely determined by the presence of underlying heart disease rather than the syncopal event itself. Population-based data from the Framingham Heart Study demonstrated that cardiac syncope is associated with significantly higher overall and cardiovascular mortality compared with vasovagal syncope. One-year mortality rates in patients with cardiac syncope range from 18 to 33%, whereas mortality in reflex syncope is generally less than 5% [[28](#B28-jcm-15-03780)]. Accordingly, current ACC/AHA/HRS and ESC guidelines emphasize early identification of high-risk cardiac features to enable timely diagnostic evaluation and therapeutic intervention, such as pacemaker implantation, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement, or corrective structural procedures, all of which may substantially reduce morbidity and mortality [[8](#B8-jcm-15-03780),[29](#B29-jcm-15-03780)]. Timely evaluation and intervention can be achieved by performing a POCCUS, such as left ventricular dysfunction, right heart strain, pericardial effusion, IVC collapsibility, and severe valvular abnormalities.

None of the widely used risk stratification rules incorporate POCCUS in the clinical decision-making algorithm. Cardiac imaging in syncope evaluation is frequently performed by cardiology consultants after patients have been admitted to the hospital. In 2017, the American College of Cardiology, American Heart Association, and the Heart Rhythm Society stated that transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) would be beneficial in patients who have an abnormal EKG or if there is a concern for structural cardiac problems or cardiac disease history [[29](#B29-jcm-15-03780)]. Subsequent evaluations of syncope patients frequently include a cardiology-performed TTE.

Baugh et al. examined the variation in testing among elderly patients presenting to the Emergency Department [[30](#B30-jcm-15-03780)]. They noted that 35% of syncope patients received an echocardiogram, and among the top five most commonly performed tests, the echocardiogram had the highest proportion of abnormal results at 22.1%. However, the echocardiogram accounted for the highest total costs at $672,648, and the cost per abnormal test is $3129, with each echocardiogram costing $514.65, but that does not factor in the associated hospitalization costs. For a limited cardiac ultrasound (CPT 93306) performed in the ED, the cost per ultrasound is lower at $481.53, according to the 2020 CMS Medicare Reimbursement rates [[31](#B31-jcm-15-03780)].

Prior studies have demonstrated emergency physicians’ ability to perform limited cardiac ultrasound to evaluate LV contractility and ejection fraction [[32](#B32-jcm-15-03780)]. In 2010, in conjunction with the American Society of Echocardiography, the American College of Emergency Physicians advocated for the use of POCCUS for the evaluation of pericardial effusion, relative chamber size, and global cardiac function [[33](#B33-jcm-15-03780)]. Given that bedside cardiac ultrasounds are one of the most commonly performed point-of-care examinations, adding this diagnostic test to the evaluation of patients with syncope is not burdensome, especially when it can reveal vital information. Acquiring a patient’s history can be difficult under various emergent circumstances, and in the elderly population, it can be even more challenging. Lindner et al. studied taking medical history of elderly patients (>75 yo) in the ED, and 25% of them could not provide a complete basic medical history (medications, past medical history, allergies, and primary care physician) [[34](#B34-jcm-15-03780)]. Past medical history can be limited, especially if the patient has not seen a physician or has limited access to care. Congestive heart failure may be first diagnosed after presenting to the ED with a syncopal episode.

Early identification of pericardial effusion using point-of-care cardiac ultrasound (POCCUS) is also crucial, particularly in hemodynamically unstable patients, as it allows rapid bedside detection of potentially life-threatening cardiac tamponade. POCCUS enables immediate visualization of pericardial fluid and assessment of hemodynamic compromise through findings such as right atrial or right ventricular diastolic collapse and inferior vena cava plethora, which are key echocardiographic features of tamponade physiology [[35](#B35-jcm-15-03780),[36](#B36-jcm-15-03780)]. In emergency and critical care settings, focused cardiac ultrasound has been shown to expedite diagnosis, guide urgent pericardiocentesis, and improve time-sensitive clinical decision-making [[37](#B37-jcm-15-03780),[38](#B38-jcm-15-03780)]. Early bedside diagnosis is therefore essential to reduce delays in intervention and potentially decrease morbidity and mortality associated with untreated cardiac tamponade [[35](#B35-jcm-15-03780)]. The development of pericardial effusion is insidious, as the patient may present with fatigue, shortness of breath, hypotension, and possibly syncope. The decision to intervene with a procedure urgently or emergently can be determined by performing POCCUS.

In the cases of suspected PE causing abnormal vital signs (tachycardia of ≥100 bpm or hypotension < 90 mmHg), focused cardiac ultrasound was 92% sensitive for PE [[39](#B39-jcm-15-03780)]. With abnormal vital signs, findings of right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) are more likely seen on POCCUS. The typical findings for RVD and elevated right-sided heart pressures are dilation of the RV, D-sign/septal flattening or bowing, McConnell’s sign, decreased tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), and with worsening RVD, tricuspid regurgitation. With PE identified in 2.2–35% of syncope patients [[24](#B24-jcm-15-03780)], performing POCCUS to evaluate for signs of RVD is well worth the time.

## 5. Future of POCCUS in Syncope Risk Stratification

Syncope risk stratification is a complex and challenging task, as evidenced by the numerous clinical decision rules and studies that have sought to validate them. In the Emergency Department, where physicians are tasked with making decisions based on limited or unreliable information, an accessible, quick, highly informative test for risk stratification can be immensely helpful. It serves as an objective, rapid bedside tool for evaluating structural and functional cardiac abnormalities that may underlie syncope. Incorporating POCCUS into clinical practice, such as left ventricular dysfunction, right heart strain, or pericardial effusion, into current clinical decision rules (CDRs) could enhance risk stratification by providing immediate physiologic data. Because of the limited literature on how well Emergency Medicine providers classify syncope with the addition of POCCUS, it is unclear how POCCUS will change risk stratification in this patient population or whether we may have been misclassifying patients with current tools. However, it can be incorporated as an additional data point into the existing syncope rules to better stratify our patients rather than a standalone tool. More research must be done in this area to improve patient outcomes and resource utilization.

[Figure 1](#fig_body_display_jcm-15-03780-f001) shows a proposed (not yet validated) algorithm incorporating POCCUS into the usual evaluation of a patient who presents with syncope and the subsequent patient disposition. After the patient with syncope presents to the ED, they will undergo a full patient history and physical examination along with EKG, blood work, etc. Then the patient will undergo a POCCUS exam. A POCCUS exam in syncope should assess for: (1) pericardial effusion/tamponade, (2) gross left ventricular dysfunction, (3) right ventricular strain (D-sign, McConnell’s sign), IVC (size, collapsibility), and (4) significant valvular abnormalities. The absence of abnormal POCCUS findings combined with stable vitals, reassuring history, normal EKG, and lack of high-risk features (overall low risk) would mean the patient can be discharged with follow-up, education, and strict return precautions. If the POCCUS is abnormal, then admission or cardiology consultation should be considered.

**Figure 1.**
Proposed point-of-care cardiac ultrasound syncope risk algorithm, which has not yet been validated.

If the patient is deemed to be an intermediate risk based on history, nonspecific EKG changes, age, and risk factors and has a normal POCCUS, then the patient could be discharged with close follow-up. If there are abnormal POCCUS findings, then admission and cardiology consultation are recommended. A normal POCCUS examination cannot independently exclude serious causes of syncope. Although point-of-care ultrasound has demonstrated utility in identifying structural and hemodynamic abnormalities in acute care settings, there is limited evidence supporting its impact on risk stratification or clinical outcomes in syncope, and its integration into standardized decision-making frameworks remains unvalidated. As such, the proposed algorithm should be considered conceptual and hypothesis-generating.

Per our protocol, if the patient is deemed high risk, the patient will need to be admitted regardless of what the POCCUS reveals, but the POCCUS may reveal a finding that would need immediate intervention, such as pericardial tamponade or severe right heart strain in PE. It can also refine differential diagnoses and guide early management in the ED or after admission. POCCUS alone does not rule out serious syncope conditions [[40](#B40-jcm-15-03780)], but it is a useful tool to increase diagnostic accuracy and augment clinical assessments.

This suggested algorithm does not comment on whether cross-sectional imaging, such as computed tomography, is needed in the patient cases. This level of medical decision-making will be deferred to the treating physician.

Although we are promoting bedside cardiac ultrasound, there are also challenges to its widespread implementation. The barriers can be qualified personnel, equipment availability, and appropriate documentation. For emergency physicians who are not trained in POCCUS or have limited experience with point-of-care ultrasound, adding this step will be challenging, as they will need to seek additional training, which can be inconsistent across institutions. The American College of Emergency Physicians recommends 25–50 quality-reviewed POCCUS to achieve proficiency [[41](#B41-jcm-15-03780)], which is challenging when there is no local expert to a provide quality-improvement review.

Point-of-care ultrasound is inherently operator-dependent, with diagnostic accuracy influenced by the clinician’s ability to acquire and interpret images, as well as integrate findings into clinical decision-making. Variability in training and experience contributes to differences in performance, even among emergency physicians [[10](#B10-jcm-15-03780)].

As mentioned previously, POCCUS findings should be interpreted within the broader clinical context of risk stratification rather than in isolation, as findings such as right ventricular dilation or reduced ejection fraction may lack specificity [[42](#B42-jcm-15-03780)]. Concerns regarding potential misdiagnosis, overuse, and inappropriate reliance on POCUS have also been raised in the literature [[42](#B42-jcm-15-03780)]. Overreliance on POCUS without appropriate clinical context may lead to diagnostic error or inappropriate management [[42](#B42-jcm-15-03780)].

Ultrasound-guided central venous catheter placement is considered the standard of care, so EDs should have an accessible ultrasound machine; however, the appropriate transducer may not be available, as the phased-array transducer is preferred for cardiac evaluation. Acquisition of an ultrasound machine or additional transducers may be cost-prohibitive, as phased-array transducers may cost over $4500 new.

Additionally, for documentation and medicolegal purposes, images of the POCCUS examinations performed should be saved and retrievable for medical record review and/or quality improvement (QI). This would require dedicated time and personnel to maintain such a repository and perform QI, both of which require expertise and financial expenditure.

## 6. Conclusions

Syncope remains a complex and high-stakes presentation in the Emergency Department, and current risk stratification tools are limited by relying on subjective history and nonspecific findings. These limitations raise concern for misclassification, particularly in patients with undiagnosed or underlying cardiac pathology.

POCCUS provides a rapid, objective bedside assessment that can identify critical conditions, including pericardial tamponade, right ventricular dysfunction, and cardiomyopathy. By providing real-time data, POCCUS can enhance diagnostic accuracy, assist medical decision-making, and improve patient disposition.

Although implementation barriers exist, they are becoming less problematic as ultrasound training and accessibility expand. POCCUS should not be viewed as a universal screening tool for syncope, but rather as a targeted adjunct in patients where structural or hemodynamic causes are suspected. Incorporating POCCUS as an adjunct to existing clinical decision rules represents a practical step toward more accurate, data-based syncope evaluation. Adoption of POCCUS in syncope assessment should be prioritized to define its role within standardized risk stratification frameworks, as it offers a meaningful opportunity to improve risk stratification, patient outcomes, and resource utilization in the Emergency Department.

# Emergency Department Management of Syncope

### About This Issue

## Transient loss of consciousness from syncope is a very common presentation in the ED, and it often has a benign etiology. Although one-third of these patients are admitted to the hospital, the majority of them will be discharged with a symptomatic diagnosis of “syncope and collapse.” A structured approach to the history, ECG assessment, risk assessment, and appropriate testing will help identify patients with life-threatening processes that do require admission. This issue will review:

## The physiologic basis for the 3 classifications: neurally mediated (reflex) syncope, orthostatic hypotension-caused syncope, and cardiac syncope

## The most common life-threatening conditions that can present with syncope

## The most helpful features to look for when differentiating seizure from syncope

## Syncope mimics: neurologic, psychiatric, metabolic, and toxicologic

## Identifying the highest risk historical features to guide disposition

## Seven of the most commonly used clinical decision tools: how do they compare, how do they differ, and are any of them useful?

## The particular concerns with elderly patients who present with syncope: falls, comorbid conditions, and underlying and undiagnosed conditions.

## The tests that all patients need to have and the tests that should be ordered only when there are specific concerns.

### Abstract

Syncope is the transient loss of consciousness and postural tone, with spontaneous recovery. It accounts for approximately 1% of all emergency department visits and $5.6 billion in healthcare costs annually. In a very small subset of patients, syncope may be a warning sign for serious outcomes or death, but identifying these patients is challenging, as the emergency clinician must distinguish between life-threatening causes and the more common, benign etiologies. Low-yield and expensive testing is often performed, even for benign presentations. Much research on syncope is observational, and clinical decision rules frequently perform poorly in validation studies. This issue reviews the clinical and diagnostic findings that are useful for safely and efficiently identifying patients presenting to the emergency department with syncope.

Given the diverse causes of pediatric syncope, routine testing in low-risk patients is costly and low-yield. # Pediatric syncope in the emergency department: a risk-stratified diagnostic and disposition pathway

## Abstract

### Background

Pediatric syncope accounts for 1–3% of emergency department (ED) visits. Although most cases are benign, 4% are caused by cardiac disease and 3% by seizures, which carry a risk of sudden death or neurologic injury if missed. Vasovagal syncope accounts for 52–74% of cases and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) for approximately 13%.

### Objective

To provide an emergency-department risk-stratified diagnostic and disposition framework for pediatric syncope.

### Key findings

A universal 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) identifies nearly all life-threatening cardiac causes of syncope. When combined with structured red-flag screening and clinical risk stratification, patients can be reliably divided into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, allowing safe discharge of benign cases and rapid admission of dangerous ones.

### Conclusion

A standardized ED syncope pathway based on risk tiers and ECG-first evaluation improves patient safety while reducing unnecessary admissions and testing.

### Clinical trial number

Not applicable.

## Introduction

Missed cardiac syncope is one of the most dangerous diagnostic failures in pediatric emergency medicine. Children presenting with transient loss of consciousness may appear well, yet a small subset harbor lethal arrhythmias or structural heart disease that can lead to sudden death if not recognized. The central challenge for the emergency physician is to rapidly identify these high-risk patients while safely discharging the majority with benign etiologies [[1](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR1 "Epping H, Müller-Schilling M, Dirrigl G, Rockmann F, Brünnler T. Syncope diagnostics in the emergency department – significance of the ESC guidelines. Med Klin Intensivmed Notfmed. 2025;15:1–7.")].

Pediatric syncope represents 1–3% of ED visits and up to 6% of adolescent hospitalizations [[2](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR2 "Ritter S, Tani LY, Etheridge SP, Williams RV, Craig JE, Minich LL. What is the yield of screening echocardiography in pediatric syncope? Pediatrics. 2000;105(5):E58."), [3](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR3 "Linzer M, Pontinen M, Gold DT, Divine GW, Felder A. Impairment of physical and psychosocial function in recurrent syncope. J Clin Epidemiol. 1991;44(10):1037–43.")]. Although most cases are reflex-mediated or orthostatic, approximately 4% are cardiac and 3% neurologic [[4](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR4 "Manouzi A, Sanatani S, Doan Q. Electrocardiogram in pediatric syncope: practice variation among pediatric emergency physicians. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2022;38(2):e886–90.")]. Because clinical appearance alone is unreliable, emergency department evaluation must be structured, protocol-driven, and anchored by early ECG screening and risk stratification [[5](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR5 "Scheier E. Cardiac POCUS in pediatric emergency medicine: a narrative review. J Clin Med. 2023;12(17):5666."), [6](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR6 "Thiruganasambandamoorthy V, Sivilotti ML, Le Sage N, Yan JW, Huang P, Hegdekar M, et al. Multicenter emergency department validation of the Canadian syncope risk score. JAMA Intern Med. 2020;180(5):737–44.")].

## Mechanisms and evidence-based framework for pediatric syncope in the ED

Pediatric syncope is a common clinical presentation in ED, with incidence peaking during adolescence and recurrence occurring in up to one-third of patients. Despite this high prevalence, fewer than 5% of cases are caused by life-threatening disease [[2](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR2 "Ritter S, Tani LY, Etheridge SP, Williams RV, Craig JE, Minich LL. What is the yield of screening echocardiography in pediatric syncope? Pediatrics. 2000;105(5):E58."), [3](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR3 "Linzer M, Pontinen M, Gold DT, Divine GW, Felder A. Impairment of physical and psychosocial function in recurrent syncope. J Clin Epidemiol. 1991;44(10):1037–43.")]. The lifetime cumulative incidence in children and adolescents is estimated to be between 15% and 25% [[7](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR7 "Colman N, Nahm K, Ganzeboom KS, et al. Epidemiology of reflex syncope. Clin Auton Res. 2004;14(Suppl 1):9–17.")]. It has a high recurrence rate and can significantly disrupt daily activities [[8](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR8 "Bhalla R, Soobhanath C, Celebi S, Chhabra M et al. Unusual Cases of Syncope in the Pediatric Age Group. 2021. Available from: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov.")]. The peak incidence occurs during adolescence (12–18 years), coinciding with rapid growth and autonomic instability [[2](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR2 "Ritter S, Tani LY, Etheridge SP, Williams RV, Craig JE, Minich LL. What is the yield of screening echocardiography in pediatric syncope? Pediatrics. 2000;105(5):E58."), [9](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR9 "Stewart JM. Common syndromes of orthostatic intolerance. Pediatrics. 2013;131(5):968–80.")]. The purpose of ED evaluation is not to identify the exact mechanism in every child, but to reliably separate dangerous causes from benign ones using a structured, evidence-based framework.

### Pathophysiological mechanisms

**Reflex (Vasovagal) Syncope (VVS)** is the most common mechanism, resulting from an inappropriate autonomic reflex leading to vasodilation and/or bradycardia, which causes transient cerebral hypoperfusion [[8](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR8 "Bhalla R, Soobhanath C, Celebi S, Chhabra M et al. Unusual Cases of Syncope in the Pediatric Age Group. 2021. Available from: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov."), [10](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR10 "Benditt DG, Nguyen JT. Vasovagal syncope: a common, benign condition. Circulation. 2009;120(18):1763–5.")]. It is often triggered by orthostatic stress, pain, or emotion and involves the Bezold–Jarisch reflex, characterized by paradoxical vagal activation [[11](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR11 "Jardine DL, Wieling W, Brignole M, et al. The pathophysiology of the vasovagal response. Heart Rhythm. 2018;15(6):921–9.")].

**Orthostatic Intolerance and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS)** are also common. Orthostatic syncope results from an inadequate autonomic response to standing, leading to venous pooling and reduced venous return [[12](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR12 "Freeman R. Clinical practice. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(6):615–24.")]. POTS, increasingly recognized in adolescents, is defined by at least 3 months of symptoms of chronic orthostatic intolerance AND a sustained excessive heart rate increase (≥ 40 beats/min in adolescents) within 10 min of standing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension [[13](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR13 "Raj SR. Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Circulation. 2013;127(23):2336–42."), [14](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR14 "Vernino S, Bourne KM, Stiles LE, Grubb BP, Fedorowski A, Stewart JM. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS): State of the science and clinical care from a 2019 National Institutes of Health Expert Consensus Meeting - Part 1. Auton Neurosci. 2021;235:102828.")].

**Cardiogenic Syncope** results from a sudden reduction in cardiac output due to structural or electrical heart disease. Although less common in children, it is the most life-threatening cause.

Arrhythmic causes include long QT syndrome, short QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (WPW), and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. While structural causes include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and coronary artery anomalies, myocarditis is also a cause of syncope/sudden death [[15](#ref-CR15 "Stephenson JB. Reflex anoxic seizures (‘white breath-holding’): nonepileptic vagal attacks. Arch Dis Child. 1978;53(3):193–200."),[16](#ref-CR16 "Friedman KG, Alexander ME. Chest pain and syncope in children: a practical approach. Pediatrics. 2013;131(5):e1530–40."),[17](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR17 "Sheldon R, Rose S, Ritchie D, Connolly S, Koshman ML, Frenneaux M. Historical criteria that distinguish syncope from seizures. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2002;40(1):142–8.")]. Syncope during exertion or without a prodrome strongly suggests a cardiac etiology.

**Other causes** include neurologic conditions that mimic syncope, such as seizures [[17](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR17 "Sheldon R, Rose S, Ritchie D, Connolly S, Koshman ML, Frenneaux M. Historical criteria that distinguish syncope from seizures. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2002;40(1):142–8.")], and metabolic disturbances like hypoglycemia [[18](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR18 "Wester M, Bergmann T, Müller-Schilling M, Maier LS, Sossalla ST. Transient hypoglycemia as a rare cause of recurring transient loss of consciousness: a case report. J Med Case Rep. 2021;15(1):261.")]. Psychogenic pseudosyncope is an important consideration in adolescents, presenting as an apparent loss of consciousness without true cerebral hypoperfusion [[19](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR19 "Gracie J, Newton JL. Psychogenic pseudosyncope: diagnosis and management. Auton Neurosci. 2014;184:66–72.")]. Figure [1](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#Fig1) illustrates the clinical classification and risk stratification of pediatric syncope with corresponding red flag categories.

![Fig. 1](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12245-026-01215-z/MediaObjects/12245_2026_1215_Fig1_HTML.png)

Clinical classification and risk stratification of pediatric syncope with corresponding red flag categories

### Synthesis of clinical practice guidelines

Several professional bodies have established guidelines for pediatric syncope. A comparison reveals a consensus on initial evaluation but differences in specific recommendations for testing and disposition. Table [1](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#Tab1) synthesizes the key recommendations from the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

### Gaps in current practice

Despite these guidelines, significant gaps in care persist. There are no universal standards for the timing and communication of ECG interpretation, and the accuracy of interpretation by non-cardiologists is variable [[24](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR24 "Fant C, Cohen A. Syncope In Pediatric Patients: A Practical Approach To Differential Diagnosis And Management In The Emergency Department. Pediatr Emerg Med Pract. 2017;14(4):1–28.")]. In the ED, patients with syncope frequently undergo extensive, low-yield testing (e.g., head CT, broad lab panels) that is inconsistent with guideline recommendations, leading to increased healthcare costs. Furthermore, outpatient follow-up rates are often low, limiting continuity of care [[25](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR25 "Conner TM, Tamirisa S, Roelle LM, Miller N, Pompa A, Orr WB, et al. Assessment of current pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation practices. Prog Pediatr Cardiol. 2024;74:101738.")].

## Red flags and high-risk features

Although most pediatric syncopal episodes are benign, early identification of red flags is essential to detect the subset of cases that are potentially life-threatening [[26](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR26 "Redd C, Thomas C, Willis M, Amos M, Anderson J. Cost of unnecessary testing in the evaluation of pediatric syncope. Pediatr Cardiol. 2017;38(6):1115–22.")].

### History-based red flags

**Cardiac red flags** [[27](#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5."),[28](#ref-CR28 "Sanatani S, Chau V, Fournier A, Dixon A, Blondin R, Sheldon RS. Canadian Cardiovascular Society and Canadian Pediatric Cardiology Association Position Statement on the Approach to Syncope in the Pediatric Patient. Can J Cardiol. 2017;33(2):189–98."),[29](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR29 "Gilpin K, Goode Z, Syncope. Pediatr Rev. 2024;45(10):606–8.")].

Syncope during exercise (mid-exertion).

Syncope while supine.

Absence of prodrome.

Chest pain or palpitations before collapse.

Known congenital or acquired heart disease.

Family history of sudden unexplained death or inherited cardiac conditions.

**Neurologic red flags**

Post-ictal confusion.

Tongue biting.

Focal or generalized convulsions.

Eye deviation.

Head trauma.

Known epilepsy.

A personal or family history of convulsive disorders should raise suspicion for a neurologic etiology [[30](#ref-CR30 "Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital. Syncope clinical pathway. Updated September 2021. [Internet]. Johns Hopkins Medicine. 2021. Available from: 
                  https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/-/media/files/allchildrens/clinical-pathways/syncope-pathway-10-6-21.pdf

**Metabolic and other red flags** [[27](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5."), [28](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR28 "Sanatani S, Chau V, Fournier A, Dixon A, Blondin R, Sheldon RS. Canadian Cardiovascular Society and Canadian Pediatric Cardiology Association Position Statement on the Approach to Syncope in the Pediatric Patient. Can J Cardiol. 2017;33(2):189–98.")].

Symptoms suggestive of hypoglycemia.

Features of severe anemia.

Features of electrolyte disturbance.

Pregnancy (in adolescents).

Possible intoxication or drug exposure.

Systemic illness or dehydration.

### Examination-based red flags

Pathologic cardiac murmurs (e.g., suggesting outflow obstruction).

Signs of heart failure.

Irregular pulse or marked bradycardia.

Abnormal blood pressure (including orthostatic hypotension).

Focal neurologic deficits.

Signs of trauma or secondary injury.

### Investigational red flags (electrocardiographic red flags)

Abnormalities on the 12-lead ECG represent critical objective markers of potential arrhythmogenic syncope.

Long QTc interval (Long QT syndrome): Long QTc (> 0.46 s in post-pubertal females, > 0.45 s in males/children),

Short QTc interval: Short QTc (< 0.32 s).

Brugada pattern (Type 1): Coved ST-segment elevation ≥ 2 mm followed by a negative T wave in ≥ 1 right precordial lead).

Pre-excitation (WPW): Short PR interval, delta wave, widened QRS.

Atrioventricular block (Mobitz II or complete heart block).

Sinus node dysfunction (inappropriate bradycardia or pauses).

Ventricular hypertrophy or repolarization abnormalities.

Clinically significant arrhythmias.

## Emergency department risk stratification

A structured approach to history-taking, physical examination, and initial investigations is crucial to stratify patients into risk categories that guide subsequent management. A focused history using high-yield questions is essential to avoid missing high-risk cases while minimizing unnecessary testing.

**High-yield history checklist**

**Pre-Attack (The 3 Ps)**:

**Position**: Was the child standing, sitting, or lying down? Was there a recent change in posture? Was the patient asleep/was there an alarm clock or phone ringing, was the patient swimming?

**Prodrome**: Were there warning symptoms (lightheadedness, nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, sense of increased OR decreased heart rate, early beats, visual changes (blurry vision, dark vision, or tunnel vision), auditory changes (buzzing, ringing, roaring, or muffled hearing).

**Provoking Factors**: Was the event triggered by pain, emotional stress, prolonged standing, heat, or dehydration, skipping meals, high free water/salt intake, venipuncture and sight of blood?

**During Attack (Witness Account)**:

**Onset**: Was it sudden or gradual?

**Duration**: How long did the loss of consciousness last?

**Appearance**: Was the fall flaccid or stiff? Was the patient awake/could the patient see/hear but not move? Were there any movements (e.g., jerking)? Was there tongue biting or incontinence?

**Post-Attack**:

**Recovery**: How long did it take to return to normal? Was there confusion or drowsiness (post-ictal state)?

**Residual Symptoms**: Was there persistent pallor, nausea, or headache?

Based on this information and initial findings, patients can be categorized using a risk stratification tool, as detailed in Table [2](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#Tab2).

## Diagnostic approach

The diagnostic approach begins with a comprehensive history and physical examination—including orthostatic vital signs, medication review, family history of sudden cardiac death, and detailed characterization of the syncopal event (triggers, prodrome, posture, and recovery)—performed prior to or in parallel with the initial ECG. This step represents the cornerstone of syncope evaluation and enables early identification of high-risk features and appropriate triage pathways, as emphasized in contemporary guideline-based approaches [[20](#ref-CR20 "Benditt DG, Cohen MI, Forman DE, Goldberger ZD, Krahn AD, Link MS, et al. 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope: executive summary. Circulation. 2017;136:e25–59."),[21](#ref-CR21 "Schunk PC, Ruttan T. Pediatric syncope approach. Emerg Med Clin North Am. 2018;36(2):349–65."),[22](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR22 "Brignole M, Moya A, de Lange FJ, Deharo JC, Elliott PM, Fanciulli A, et al. 2018 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J. 2018;39(21):1883–948."), [24](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR24 "Fant C, Cohen A. Syncope In Pediatric Patients: A Practical Approach To Differential Diagnosis And Management In The Emergency Department. Pediatr Emerg Med Pract. 2017;14(4):1–28.")].

The ECG is the first diagnostic test in all pediatric syncope. No child should be dispositioned without a documented ECG review. The ED physician must interpret and document the 12-lead ECG before disposition, with a pediatric cardiologist over-read within 24–48 h. A standardized recall system should ensure families are promptly contacted if concerning findings arise. High parasternal leads (V1–V2) may be used selectively when Brugada syndrome is suspected, also the long QTc interval must manually verified, as automated algorithms often overestimate QT, especially with U waves [[4](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR4 "Manouzi A, Sanatani S, Doan Q. Electrocardiogram in pediatric syncope: practice variation among pediatric emergency physicians. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2022;38(2):e886–90."), [22](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR22 "Brignole M, Moya A, de Lange FJ, Deharo JC, Elliott PM, Fanciulli A, et al. 2018 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J. 2018;39(21):1883–948."), [28](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR28 "Sanatani S, Chau V, Fournier A, Dixon A, Blondin R, Sheldon RS. Canadian Cardiovascular Society and Canadian Pediatric Cardiology Association Position Statement on the Approach to Syncope in the Pediatric Patient. Can J Cardiol. 2017;33(2):189–98.")].

If POTS is suspected (syncope with chronic orthostatic symptoms), perform a standardized 10-minute standing test: after 5 min supine rest with baseline HR/BP, the patient stands while HR and BP are recorded every minute for 10 min, in a quiet setting with minimal movement and no leaning [[33](#ref-CR33 "Singhi P, Saini AG. Syncope in Pediatric Practice. Indian J Pediatr. 2018;85:636–40."),[34](#ref-CR34 "Sutton R, Ricci F, Fedorowski A. Risk stratification of syncope: Current syncope guidelines and beyond. Auton Neurosci. 2022;238:102929."),[35](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR35 "Wang C, Liao Y, Wang S, Tian H, Huang M, Dong XY, et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of neurally mediated syncope in children and adolescents (Revised 2024). World J Pediatr. 2024;20(10):983–1002.")].

Following this initial assessment, patients are categorized into “presumptive diagnosis,” “suggestive diagnosis,” and “unclassified,” which should be clarified as transitional diagnostic states reflecting the degree of diagnostic certainty rather than formal risk categories, consistent with contemporary risk-stratification frameworks [[6](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR6 "Thiruganasambandamoorthy V, Sivilotti ML, Le Sage N, Yan JW, Huang P, Hegdekar M, et al. Multicenter emergency department validation of the Canadian syncope risk score. JAMA Intern Med. 2020;180(5):737–44."), [22](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR22 "Brignole M, Moya A, de Lange FJ, Deharo JC, Elliott PM, Fanciulli A, et al. 2018 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Auton Neurosci. 2022;238:102929.")].

The “presumptive diagnosis” group includes patients with clinically evident benign etiologies - most commonly reflex syncope, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or orthostatic hypotension - which can often be diagnosed based on history and examination alone [[9](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR9 "Stewart JM. Common syndromes of orthostatic intolerance. Pediatrics. 2013;131(5):968–80."), [10](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR10 "Benditt DG, Nguyen JT. Vasovagal syncope: a common, benign condition. Circulation. 2009;120(18):1763–5."), [13](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR13 "Raj SR. Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Circulation. 2013;127(23):2336–42.")]. The “suggestive diagnosis” category includes cases with features concerning for cardiac pathology, prompting further evaluation with echocardiography and ambulatory rhythm monitoring to establish a definitive diagnosis [[2](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR2 "Ritter S, Tani LY, Etheridge SP, Williams RV, Craig JE, Minich LL. What is the yield of screening echocardiography in pediatric syncope? Pediatrics. 2000;105(5):E58."), [21](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR21 "Schunk PC, Ruttan T. Pediatric syncope approach. Emerg Med Clin North Am. 2018;36(2):349–65."), [36](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR36 "Pradhan S, Robinson JA, Shivapour JK, Snyder CS. Ambulatory arrhythmia detection with zio® xt patch in pediatric patients: a comparison of devices. Pediatr Cardiol. 2019;40(5):921–4.")]. The “unclassified” group comprises patients with inconclusive initial evaluation, requiring additional targeted testing for less common metabolic, neurological, or psychogenic causes [[18](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR18 "Wester M, Bergmann T, Müller-Schilling M, Maier LS, Sossalla ST. Transient hypoglycemia as a rare cause of recurring transient loss of consciousness: a case report. J Med Case Rep. 2021;15(1):261."), [19](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR19 "Gracie J, Newton JL. Psychogenic pseudosyncope: diagnosis and management. Auton Neurosci. 2014;184:66–72."), [23](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR23 "National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral. NICE guideline [NG127]. London: NICE; 2023.")].

Laboratory testing should be limited to glucose and pregnancy testing, with additional studies ordered only when clinically indicated. Routine imaging, including chest X-ray and head CT, is not part of standard syncope evaluation [[35](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR35 "Wang C, Liao Y, Wang S, Tian H, Huang M, Dong XY, et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of neurally mediated syncope in children and adolescents (Revised 2024). World J Pediatr. 2024;20(10):983–1002."), [37](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR37 "Zhu W, Bian X, Lv J. Advances in diagnosis, management, and long-term outcomes of pediatric vasovagal syncope: a comprehensive review. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2025;12:1481749.")].

Targeted laboratory testing is recommended over broad panels. A point-of-care blood glucose measurement is essential to rule out hypoglycemia, which can mimic syncope [[18](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR18 "Wester M, Bergmann T, Müller-Schilling M, Maier LS, Sossalla ST. Transient hypoglycemia as a rare cause of recurring transient loss of consciousness: a case report. J Med Case Rep. 2021;15(1):261.")]. A pregnancy test is required for all adolescent females due to the physiological changes of pregnancy that can precipitate syncope [[37](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR37 "Zhu W, Bian X, Lv J. Advances in diagnosis, management, and long-term outcomes of pediatric vasovagal syncope: a comprehensive review. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2025;12:1481749.")]. Other labs, such as a complete blood count (CBC) to check for anemia or a metabolic panel for electrolyte disturbances, or urine drug/toxins screen should be ordered selectively based on clinical suspicion [[38](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR38 "Javier RC, Singh PV, Shrestha J, Abdalla R, Narang P, Patel H, et al. Trends and immediate outcomes of syncope during pregnancy: a narrative review. Cureus. 2023;15(12):e49833."), [39](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR39 "Hatharasinghe AT, Etebar K, Wolsky R, Akhondi H, Ayutyanont N. An assessment of the diagnostic value in syncope workup: a retrospective study. HCA Healthc J Med. 2021;2(6):423–31.")].

More selective testing is reserved for intermediate- or high-risk patients. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) may be considered conditionally at the bedside to assess for gross structural abnormalities like significant pericardial effusion or severe left ventricular dysfunction, but it is not a routine part of the initial workup [[5](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR5 "Scheier E. Cardiac POCUS in pediatric emergency medicine: a narrative review. J Clin Med. 2023;12(17):5666."), [40](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR40 "Johri AM, Glass C, Hill B, Jensen T, Puentes W, Olusanya O, et al. The evolution of cardiovascular ultrasound: a review of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (Pocus) across specialties. Am J Med. 2023;136(7):621–8.")]. For patients with high-risk features or abnormal ECGs, continuous telemetry monitoring is required [[18](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR18 "Wester M, Bergmann T, Müller-Schilling M, Maier LS, Sossalla ST. Transient hypoglycemia as a rare cause of recurring transient loss of consciousness: a case report. J Med Case Rep. 2021;15(1):261.")]. Ambulatory monitors like a Holter monitor (24–48 h) or a Zio patch (up to 14 days), or event monitors/recorders worn for up to 30 days are useful for diagnosing intermittent arrhythmias in patients with recurrent, unexplained episodes [[35](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR35 "Wang C, Liao Y, Wang S, Tian H, Huang M, Dong XY, et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of neurally mediated syncope in children and adolescents (Revised 2024). World J Pediatr. 2024;20(10):983–1002."), [36](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR36 "Pradhan S, Robinson JA, Shivapour JK, Snyder CS. Ambulatory arrhythmia detection with zio® xt patch in pediatric patients: a comparison of devices. Pediatr Cardiol. 2019;40(5):921–4.")].

The diagnostic algorithm (Fig. [2](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#Fig2)) should follow a risk-based sequence. For low-risk patients with a normal ECG and clear vasovagal history, the disposition is typically discharge with education. For intermediate-risk patients (e.g., recurrent episodes, atypical features), further testing like ambulatory monitoring and specialist referral is appropriate. For high-risk patients (e.g., abnormal ECG, exertional syncope), the disposition is admission for inpatient monitoring and urgent specialist consultation. Neurological red flags warrant an EEG and neurology referral to differentiate syncope from seizure [[18](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR18 "Wester M, Bergmann T, Müller-Schilling M, Maier LS, Sossalla ST. Transient hypoglycemia as a rare cause of recurring transient loss of consciousness: a case report. J Med Case Rep. 2021;15(1):261.")]. Finally, the algorithm emphasizes iterative reassessment and selective referral, ensuring a dynamic, resource-conscious approach that optimizes diagnostic yield while avoiding unnecessary investigations [[24](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR24 "Fant C, Cohen A. ## Common final diagnoses

Analysis of pediatric syncope presentations to the ED consistently demonstrates that reflex and orthostatic etiologies predominate. Vasovagal syncope is the most frequent diagnosis, accounting for 52.5% to 74% of cases, followed by postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) at approximately 13.1% [[27](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5."), [41](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR41 "Libdeh AA, Al-Ammouri I, Otoom G, Chabaan R, Tutunji L, Phillips LH 2, et al. Pediatric syncope in specialty clinics: clinical characteristics and lessons learned. Int J Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2025;12(4):179–83."), [42](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR42 "Shenk MER, Anilkumar A. Syncope in children: etiology, positive and negative predictors, and utilization and utility of diagnostic testing (P3.204). Neurology. 2017;88(16 Suppl):P3204.")]. In contrast, serious etiologies are uncommon, with cardiac causes identified in ~ 4% and neurological causes (primarily seizures) in ~ 3.1% of cases [[27](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5.")].

### Benign etiologies (Reflex and orthostatic causes)

Vasovagal syncope and POTS are the most common final diagnoses and are considered benign. In multiple retrospective studies, VVS was the leading cause, identified in over 70% of patients in some cohorts [[41](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR41 "Libdeh AA, Al-Ammouri I, Otoom G, Chabaan R, Tutunji L, Phillips LH 2, et al. Pediatric syncope in specialty clinics: clinical characteristics and lessons learned. Int J Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2025;12(4):179–83."), [42](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR42 "Shenk MER, Anilkumar A. Syncope in children: etiology, positive and negative predictors, and utilization and utility of diagnostic testing (P3.204). Neurology. 2017;88(16 Suppl):P3204.")]. Although these conditions are not life-threatening, they can cause significant disruption to a child’s life. A quality improvement initiative suggested that for these low-risk patients, adequate history gathering, physical exam, and a baseline ECG are sufficient for diagnosis, and extensive, costly testing does not improve patient outcomes [[43](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR43 "Winder MM, Marietta J, Kerr LM, Puchalski MD, Zhang C, Ware AL, et al. Reducing unnecessary diagnostic testing in pediatric syncope: a quality improvement initiative. Pediatr Cardiol. 2021;42(4):942–50.")].

### Serious etiologies (Cardiac and neurological causes)

Although rare, serious causes corresponding to the high-risk categories are rare but clinically critical to identify. Cardiac causes account for approximately 4% of cases, with arrhythmias representing the most common subtype (16.9% of cardiac cases), while inherited channelopathies (e.g., long QT syndrome) and cardiomyopathies are considerably less frequent (3.4% and < 2%, respectively) [[27](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5.")]. Patients with clinical features suggestive of cardiac syncope (as defined by red flags in Sect. [Gaps in current practice](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#Sec5)) require urgent cardiology evaluation, often including hospital admission for continuous monitoring and consideration of advanced therapies (e.g., ablation or device implantation). Conversely, patients with isolated concerning family history but otherwise normal ED evaluation may be safely managed with expedited outpatient cardiology follow-up within 48–72 h, following direct specialist consultation [[27](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5.")]. Neurological etiologies, primarily seizures misclassified as syncope, account for approximately 3.1% of cases. Other rare but important diagnoses—including anemia, trauma, and intracranial hemorrhage—each contribute to less than 1% of presentations [[27](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR27 "Zavala R, Metais B, Tuckfield L, DelVecchio M, Aronoff S. Pediatric Syncope: A Systematic Review. Pediatr Emerg Care. 2020;36(9):442–5.")].

## Disposition framework

Current recommendations for addressing pediatric syncope are consensus-based, meaning timelines are derived from clinical convention rather than evidence-based trials [[33](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR33 "Singhi P, Saini AG. Syncope in Pediatric Practice. Indian J Pediatr. 2018;85:636–40.")]. Therefore, careful risk stratification is needed for assessing syncope severity and determining disposition, such as identifying which cases may be managed as an outpatient versus those that require inpatient observation. The disposition decision should be directly linked to the risk tier identified during the initial evaluation.

### Low-risk tier disposition

Patients with diagnoses such as vasovagal syncope and POTS are generally classified as low-risk typically safe for ED discharge, they frequently require acute symptom management with parenteral saline in the ED. Furthermore, discharge planning must include comprehensive education on managing their wide array of systemic symptoms (beyond just presyncope) focusing on trigger avoidance, recognition of presyncope symptoms, and counter-pressure maneuvers. Maintaining adequate oral hydration and increasing salt intake has been shown to be an imperative and effective step in treatment, significantly reducing recurrence rates and a direct referral to a specialist or clinic familiar with the multidisciplinary care of POTS [[33](#ref-CR33 "Singhi P, Saini AG. Syncope in Pediatric Practice. Indian J Pediatr. 2018;85:636–40."),[34](#ref-CR34 "Sutton R, Ricci F, Fedorowski A. Risk stratification of syncope: Current syncope guidelines and beyond. Auton Neurosci. 2022;238:102929."),[35](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR35 "Wang C, Liao Y, Wang S, Tian H, Huang M, Dong XY, et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of neurally mediated syncope in children and adolescents (Revised 2024). World J Pediatr. 2024;20(10):983–1002.")].

### Intermediate-risk tier disposition

Disposition for intermediate-risk cases requires systematic evaluation. Observation or admission may be considered if the clinical presentation suggests a strong likelihood of early complications. Otherwise, patients may be discharged with structured follow-up visits, generally within 1–2 weeks, to a specialized syncope clinic or an appropriate specialist (e.g., neurology for suspected seizures, cardiology for recurrent episodes without clear red flags) [[33](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR33 "Singhi P, Saini AG. Syncope in Pediatric Practice. Indian J Pediatr. 2018;85:636–40."), [34](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR34 "Sutton R, Ricci F, Fedorowski A. Risk stratification of syncope: Current syncope guidelines and beyond. Auton Neurosci. 2022;238:102929.")].

### High-risk tier disposition

Children who fall into the high-risk tier, such as those with exertional syncope, abnormal ECG findings, or a concerning family history, warrant hospital admission for further targeted testing, continuous monitoring, and urgent cardiology or neurology evaluation [[33](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR33 "Singhi P, Saini AG. Syncope in Pediatric Practice. Indian J Pediatr. 2018;85:636–40."), [44](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR44 "Wang Y, Wang Y, Li X, Du J, Zhang H, Jin H, et al. Efficacy of increased salt and water intake on pediatric vasovagal syncope: a meta-analysis based on global published data. Front Pediatr. 2021;9:663016.")]. This approach ensures that patients with potentially life-threatening conditions receive prompt and comprehensive inpatient management.

## Research agenda

Future research should prioritize the large-scale validation of pediatric syncope clinical decision rules. Current guidelines are largely consensus-based, and there is limited evidence that existing rules can be reliably generalized to safely identify low-risk children for discharge while accurately detecting dangerous etiologies [[34](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR34 "Sutton R, Ricci F, Fedorowski A. Risk stratification of syncope: Current syncope guidelines and beyond. Auton Neurosci. 2022;238:102929.")]. Prospective studies are needed to substantiate the role of emerging technologies like POCUS in refining risk stratification at the bedside [[45](/article/10.1186/s12245-026-01215-z#ref-CR45 "Lin-Martore M, Kornblith A, Firnberg M, Haque A, O’Brien B. Trust of artificial intelligence-augmented point-of-care ultrasound among pediatric emergency medicine physicians. J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open. 2025;6(4):100173.")]. Given the diverse causes of pediatric syncope, routine testing in low-risk patients is costly and low-yield. Therefore, future studies should focus on the cost-effectiveness of targeted, minimalist diagnostic algorithms that prioritize safety and resource stewardship by forgoing unnecessary laboratory investigations, imaging, and admissions in low-risk patients.

## Conclusion

Pediatric syncope must be managed as an emergency-department safety problem. A risk-stratified, ECG-first pathway ensures that children with cardiac or neurologic disease are rapidly identified and admitted while benign cases are safely discharged. Emergency departments should implement standardized syncope pathways based on red flags, ECG findings, and disposition tiers to reduce missed diagnoses and unnecessary hospitalizations.
